M09.1:
Scheduled visit at North Star Neurology, thirty minutes, held in the shared workroom between afternoon appt blocks. I opened by confirming that the package sent after our January interaction had arrived and had been read by the nursing staff as well.

The substantive part of the discussion concerned a shift the practice has noticed since the stroke service at the affiliated hospital expanded. Described a growing cluster of post-stroke epilepsy patients and asked what evidence exists for cenobamate in that setting. I said plainly that I could not speak beyond the approved labeling, which covers adults with focal onset seizures, and that I would return with whatever published literature exists on that population rather than characterizing it myself. The response was understanding, and the ask was framed as a literature question rather than a treatment request.

Two further items were raised. First, the interaction checking references we discussed in January should be in a form the pharmacy team can circulate internally. Second, a request to be notified when the spring regional meeting agenda is published.

Follow-ups on my side are as follows: (1) submit the literature request to Medical Information this week, (2) confirm receipt of whatever comes back, and (3) log the unresolved question in the interaction system for field team review. No safety items were reported; I asked before closing and the answer was none. Next contact planned for April, in person.

M10.1:
Visit on March 2 at Silver Peak Clinic in Reno, 25 minutes, third interaction with this office since September 2025. The panel was described as roughly 40 percent over age 65, which matches what the practice manager told me in December.

Most of the conversation stayed on prescribing in older adults. Avoids starting older adults unless a pharmacist reviews the full medication list first, citing DDI concerns. The clinic has a pharmacist on site two days a week, Tuesday and Thursday, so that review step can add seven to ten days before any new ASM is started, and in practice a share of pts do not return for the f/u appt inside that window. Noted that the same caution is applied across the ASM class rather than to any single agent.

Asked whether a short interaction reference exists that a non-specialist could use during the visit itself. I confirmed I would check what is available through Medical Information and would not summarize labeling from memory. No dosing was discussed.

No safety events were reported today; I asked directly and the answer was none.

Follow-ups: request the interaction reference by March 9, and confirm the next appointment for the week of April 20. Logged for internal tracking that in this practice the rate limiting step is pharmacy review capacity, not any question about the medication itself.

M11.1:
Drop-in at Redwood Basin, ~15 min in the hallway betwen clinic blocks. Second visit this quarter.

Opened with schedule talk. Office is running 2 wks behind on new pt appts, so f/u intervals have stretched. Nothing I can do there, noted it anyway.

Brought up an adult who stopped the drug unprompted after a week of feeling foggy and unusually sleepy. I did not probe for clinical detail. Told the prescriber I would route this through the safety process the same day and that the safety group may follow up directly. Confirmed the pt is being seen again soon. Nothing further volunteered on that case and I did not ask.

Rest of the visit was general. Complaint about the EHR again, same as last time — the template has no clean field for seizure counts so nursing free texts it. Also asked whether the CNB materials from the last visit had circulated; answer was the front desk still has the packet.

No data requests today. No promotional discussion. Stayed at label level, no dosing talk.

Next steps: safety intake submitted 3/23, coordinator to confirm a longer sit-down appt, plan to check back in May. Note for the team that hallway visits are all this office can give until the backlog clears.

M12.1:
A scheduled forty-minute meeting at the Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, in the conference room adjoining the monitoring unit, with a fellow present for the first half at the invitation of the attending.

Much of the conversation was a look back over the past year in the refractory adult clinic. Said several DRE adults in the panel finally responded after years of cycling medications. I asked, as neutrally as I could, how many patients that impression was drawn from, and the answer was a handful followed over roughly three quarters, tracked in seizure diaries rather than in any formal audit. Went as far as saying it works for every patient tried on it so far. I did not reinforce that framing, and I have noted for the record that this is a single-center impression from a small number of patients and not something I can carry forward as a general statement.

We also touched on the reimbursement paperwork burden, which the institute finds heaviest for the prior authorization step, and on interest in contributing to investigator-initiated work. I said the research interest belongs with the appropriate internal team rather than with me.

Two follow-ups: route the research interest to that team this week, and confirm the June visit once the fellowship schedule is posted. No safety items were raised; I asked before leaving. The tone throughout was collegial and generous with time.

M13.1:
Short visit, Flint Hills office in Wichita. 12 min, standing, betwen afternoon blocks. Rescheduled twice before this one.

Main topic was volume. Practice is seeing more new pts this quarter than last, about a third more by the front desk count, mostly referrals from two family medicine groups that lost their own neuro coverage in the spring. Panel is skewing older as a result. Mix has shifted toward general follow up work and away from procedures.

Knock on effect is scheduling. New pt slots now 6 wks out. Some routine f/u appt intervals stretched to 9 months, which the practice is not happy about. Chart prep runs into lunch most days.

Second half was the EHR build. Seizure frequency is still a free text field, so nobody can pull counts across the panel without reading every note. Nursing keeps a paralell spreadsheet, which the practice manager wants stopped. I said I hear the same complaint in other offices but have no template to offer and would not advise on their build.

Nothing clinical raised. No materials requested, none left. No product discussion at all this visit, and I did not introduce any. No safety items; asked and confirmed none.

Next: check back after the vendor training in January.

M14.1:
Brief in-person visit at Green Mountain Neuroscience on the afternoon of December 22, arranged around a shortened holiday clinic schedule. I had offered to make this a phone call, but the office preferred to meet while I was already in Burlington.

The conversation was almost entirely logistical and concerned the spring regional epilepsy meeting. The practice expects to send two clinicians and one nurse practitioner, contingent on coverage; the difficulty is that the meeting falls on a Thursday and Friday, which are the two heaviest clinic days here. Registration is open, but the group rate at the conference hotel closes in mid-January and the travel budget has not yet been confirmed by the practice manager. I was asked, informally, which sessions tend to fill first and whether the poster hall justifies the extra day. I answered in general terms and made no commitments.

We also discussed who else from the region is likely to attend. Two colleagues from a neighboring practice are apparently going, and there was interest in coordinating ground travel from the airport.

No clinical or product topics were raised by either party, and no materials were requested or left. There were no safety items to report; I confirmed this before closing.

My follow-ups: (1) forward the published agenda once it is posted, (2) propose a first-quarter meeting date after the January clinic calendar is finalized, and (3) thank the coordinator who arranged this visit on short notice.

M15.1:
Visit on May 27 at Prairie Gate Health in Des Moines, 30 minutes in the office at the end of the morning clinic. Fourth interaction with this practice since October 2025, third since January.

The clinic sits downstream of two pediatric neurology practices and takes transition-age patients at 18, and that referral pattern framed most of the discussion. Asked me to flag internally that adolescent refractory focal epilepsy keeps coming up with no on-label answer for those families. I recorded the comment as stated. To be explicit for the record: the request was to log the gap, not to use any product outside its approved population, and I said clearly that the approval covers adults 18 and older and that I would not discuss use below that age.

Separately, two of the four scheduled pts today were transition visits, which the coordinator says is up from last year, and the practice tracks pending transitions on a shared calendar. There was also a short complaint about prior authorization paperwork generally, with no product specifics.

Follow-ups: log the unresolved question in the interaction system today, route the adolescent evidence question to Medical Information, and confirm the next visit for the week of July 13. No safety items reported; asked and confirmed none.

M16.1:
First visit of the year, Palmetto Neurology in Charleston. 20 min in the back office. Coordinator sat in for part of it.

Staffing is the whole story here. Practice lost 2 MAs in November and has not backfilled. One of the two front desk staff is out on leave until February. Result is a new pt backlog at ~9 wks, up from 5 in the fall. Routine f/u appt slots keep getting pushed, and some pts are rescheduling themselves out past 6 months.

Triage is now handled by whoever picks up the phone, which the practice knows is not sustainable. They are looking at sharing an MA with the sleep group upstairs. Also mentioned the holiday week wiped out 3 clinic days and that catch up will take most of January.

Asked about my travel schedule, since my visits keep landing on their busiest days. Agreed to try late Monday afternoons going foward.

Nothing clinical came up. No materials requested, none left. No product discussion this visit. No safety items; asked and confirmed none.

Next: coordinator to send Q1 availability, I check back mid Feb. Note for the team that this office has little bandwidth for meetings until the MA roles are filled.

M17.1:
A pleasant thirty-five minute meeting at Harborlight Neurology in Portland, the second since the practice moved into the new suite, and the first at which the office pharmacist was able to join for part of the time.

Elderly polypharmacy came up again, with a request for education materials to hand to caregivers. This has now been raised at three of my last four visits here, and I mention it because the framing has shifted slightly. The concern is less about any single interaction than about a caregiver having to keep track of a long list at home, often across two or three prescribers, and then explain the schedule to a spouse or an adult child who does not attend the appt. The specific ask was for something plain-language and printable, not written for clinicians.

I explained that I could not produce such a piece myself, that I would route the request through the appropriate internal team, and that I could make no commitment on timing. We agreed the request would be logged as stated.

Otherwise the visit was uneventful. Patient volume was described as steady this quarter, a little heavier on new referrals, and there was the usual complaint about parking at the new building. No safety matters were raised; I asked, and the answer was none. I plan to follow up in July.
